This is **base-promoted N-ethoxycarbonyl deprotection of a piperazine**:

\[
\text{N-CO}_2\text{Et piperazine} \rightarrow \text{secondary piperazine} + \text{CO}_2\text{-derived/ethanol-containing byproducts}
\]

The ethoxycarbonyl group attached to one piperazine nitrogen is removed, generating the corresponding **N–H piperazine**. The fused N–N heteroaromatic system, aryl fluoride, and all core C–N bonds remain unchanged.

This is consistent with **alkaline carbamate hydrolysis/deprotection**, often described operationally as removal of an ethoxycarbonyl protecting group under aqueous alcoholic basic conditions.

The reaction removes the piperazine-bound **ethoxycarbonyl carbamate**:

\[
\mathrm{N{-}CO_2Et \rightarrow N{-}H}
\]

The fused heteroaromatic system, aryl fluoride, and remaining C–N bonds are retained. Thus, this is **carbamate hydrolysis/deprotection**, not a cyclization, aryl fluoride substitution, or elimination.

### Other plausible reagent systems

If the exact precedent were unavailable, chemically plausible alternatives would include:

- **Aqueous NaOH or LiOH**, often with an alcohol cosolvent
- **Hydrazine hydrate**, for base-sensitive carbamate cleavage in some cases

However, the highest-confidence assignment is:

> **KOH, water, and 1-methoxyethanol; heat may have been used to promote alkaline carbamate hydrolysis.**

The ethoxycarbonyl group should not be called Cbz: **Cbz is benzyloxycarbonyl**, whereas this substrate contains an **ethoxycarbonyl (carbamate) protecting group**.
